claims.text: Reducing FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle diameter lowers the temperature at which significant atomic rearrangements occur.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower overall thermal stability than larger ones.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are chemically disordered, nearly random solid solutions.
Hybrid molecular-dynamics/Monte Carlo simulation can be used to study the evolution of chemical ordering as a function of temperature.
Aberration-corrected in situ TEM can be used to study the thermal response of these nanoparticles up to approximately 1000 K.
An inert atmosphere or vacuum prevents oxidation during heating.
Heating FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles produces chemical short-range order.
Ordered clusters form within FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles during thermal treatment.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio promotes surface diffusion in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The surfaces of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles reduce the energy barrier for atomic rearrangements.
Enhanced surface diffusion and reduced rearrangement barriers cause ordering or phase transitions at lower temperatures.
Smaller nanoparticles develop new diffraction features or lattice-parameter changes at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles exhibit increased atomic displacement at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles undergo morphological evolution at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
At room temperature, all nanoparticle sizes preserve a random chemical arrangement and stable lattice structure.
The proposed size effect is prominent only when oxidation and external contamination are negligible.
The proposed size effect may not apply to nanoparticles containing significant pre-existing defects.
Exact transition temperatures and ordering kinetics may vary with synthesis quality and measurement resolution.
